title: [Python] Segmentation fault occurs on libarrow load when using the pyarrow 17.0.0 arm64 wheel
body: Importing PyArrow 17.0.0 from the ARM wheel can reliably segfault in my application when libarrow.so is loaded. Under gdb, the crashing thread is jemalloc_bg_thd in jemalloc's background_thread_entry. This only happens on ARM, goes away if I downgrade PyArrow, and is extremely sensitive to the order in which other Python extension modules are imported before PyArrow. Reordering or adding an unrelated import can make it disappear. Rebuilding and preloading libarrow.so also made the crash disappear, so I have not been able to obtain a useful debug build.

symptoms_visible: My application reliably segfaults while loading libarrow.so from the PyArrow 17.0.0 ARM wheel after several other Python extension modules have been imported.
The gdb backtrace stops in background_thread_entry on a thread named jemalloc_bg_thd.
Downgrading PyArrow avoids the crash, while changing the order of unrelated imports can also make it disappear.
N0.label: N0 ARM import-order-sensitive crash reported

symptoms_visible: The same ARM wheel test still segfaults after I configure PyArrow to use mimalloc.
N1.label: N1 alternate allocator selected but crash remains

symptoms_visible: With the latest nightly wheel, running the application import sequence still segfaults with the same jemalloc_bg_thd backtrace.
Starting a fresh interpreter and importing only pyarrow succeeds.
N2.label: N2 nightly reproduces only after prior imports

symptoms_visible: The complex import sequence segfaults with both PyArrow 17.0.0 and the current nightly, while it works with PyArrow versions older than 17.0.0.
N2_x.label: N2_x no-PyArrow-action brush-off rejected

symptoms_visible: The failing import sequence completes successfully with the provided ARM candidate wheel.
After I reinstall PyArrow 17.0.0, the same command segfaults again.
N3.label: N3 candidate wheel verified by downgrade comparison

symptoms_visible: The previously failing extension-module import sequence completes without a segmentation fault when I use an ARM wheel built without jemalloc.
N_terminal.label: terminal ARM wheel no longer crashes

question_patterns: Can you select a different supported memory allocator and rerun the failing workflow?
Please change the configured allocator, then report whether the same import sequence still crashes.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I configured the allocator to mimalloc in the linked workflow, but the ARM wheel test still segfaults.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: After selecting mimalloc, the same import sequence runs reliably without a segfault.
The command still segfaults with mimalloc selected, but the thread number differs between runs.

edges.comment: Reporter system, c3-c5: a maintainer suggested selecting mimalloc, and the reporter tested that configuration in the affected ARM CI job. The reporter supplied only the observed continued segfault; the conclusion that merely selecting another allocator does not prevent linked jemalloc code from loading is engineer-side.

question_patterns: Could you install the latest nightly wheel and rerun the exact failing import sequence?
Please compare the full application import sequence with importing PyArrow by itself on the latest nightly.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With PyArrow 18.0.0.dev445, `python -c "import cupy; import cudf;"` still exits with `Segmentation fault (core dumped)`, and the backtrace is still in jemalloc_bg_thd. In a fresh interpreter, `import pyarrow` by itself succeeds and reports version `18.0.0.dev445`.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The exact application sequence succeeds on the nightly in repeated runs, although PyArrow 17.0.0 still crashes.
The nightly still crashes only after the same prior extension imports, but its development version number is a few builds newer.

edges.comment: Reporter system, c7-c15: maintainers requested a nightly-wheel test. The reporter unexpectedly reproduced the crash and supplied the raw commands, version, and differing outcomes for the complex sequence and direct import.

solution.intent: Conclude that no PyArrow change is warranted because importing PyArrow alone succeeds and the crash requires a complicated third-party dependency sequence.
solution.concrete_example: Since `import pyarrow` alone does not crash, treat the problem as belonging to the surrounding dependency stack rather than changing the PyArrow wheel.

edges.comment: Reporter system, c11-c15: a maintainer asked whether there was anything particular for PyArrow to do after learning that a direct import succeeds. The reporter rejected that brush-off with the version correlation: pre-17 works, while both 17.0.0 and the nightly fail under the reproducible application sequence.

question_patterns: Could you install this provided aarch64 wheel and rerun the exact command that currently crashes?
Please test the candidate wheel against the failing sequence, then compare it with the released wheel if possible.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I installed the provided Python 3.12 aarch64 wheel, `pyarrow-18.0.0.dev452-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl`, and `python -c "import cupy; import cudf;"` completed normally. I then reinstalled PyArrow 17.0.0 and ran the same command again; it printed `Segmentation fault (core dumped)`.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The provided candidate wheel still segfaults on the same command, just like PyArrow 17.0.0.
The candidate succeeds and the released wheel crashes again, but I tested from a different working directory.

edges.comment: Reporter system, c16 and c23: the reporter tested a Python 3.12 artifact from the candidate build, then deliberately downgraded to 17.0.0 to reconfirm the failure. This is a pre-resolution candidate-build measurement. The build property that distinguishes the artifact is kept out of the raw user answer and inferred on the final solution edge.

solution.intent: Build Linux ARM PyArrow wheels without jemalloc and use the resulting wheel instead of relying on a runtime allocator selection, because loading the statically bundled jemalloc code is implicated in the import-time crash.
solution.concrete_example: Disable jemalloc when producing the Linux aarch64 wheel, ship the wheel with that build-time change, and have the affected user rerun the previously failing extension import sequence before declaring the issue resolved.
solution.inference_hint: Maintainers know that the successful candidate artifact was built with jemalloc disabled. Comparing that artifact with the renewed failure after downgrading implicates the presence of statically linked jemalloc in the ARM wheel. The thread does not establish a more precise internal jemalloc mechanism, so an agent should not claim that page size, TLS layout, or a particular jemalloc source line was proven as the original reporter's root cause.

edges.comment: Original reporter's diagnostic chain, c16-c23: maintainers built and merged the ARM-wheel change, and the reporter verified the corresponding candidate artifact against the exact failing command with a downgrade control. Later x86 reports describe separate deployments and are intentionally excluded from this ARM resolution chain.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted cause at the level established by the thread: the Linux ARM wheel's statically bundled jemalloc is implicated in the import-time jemalloc background-thread crash; the precise internal jemalloc defect was not proven.
Must recommend disabling or omitting jemalloc at build time for Linux ARM wheels, rather than treating runtime selection of mimalloc as sufficient.
Diagnosis must be grounded in the gdb backtrace, the continued crash after selecting mimalloc, the nightly reproduction, and the successful candidate-wheel versus released-wheel downgrade comparison.

Must not dismiss the issue merely because `import pyarrow` succeeds in isolation; the reporter reproducibly triggered it after a specific sequence of extension-module imports and correlated it with PyArrow wheel versions.
Must have the affected reporter verify the exact failing import sequence on a wheel containing the build-time change before treating the issue as resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly technical Python and native-extension developer who can inspect shared-library loading with strace, collect full gdb backtraces, modify CI workflows, install wheel artifacts, and reason cautiously about allocators and symbol interactions.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, precise, cooperative, and evidence-driven; clearly separates observations from hypotheses, quotes commands and outputs, and challenges tentative conclusions with controlled comparisons.
